Relevance as a Vulnerability: How Web Retrieval Degrades Safety Alignment in LLM Agents
Warning: This paper may include model-generated content that could be considered offensive.

Aditya Nawal Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering    Manit Baser Affiliation: National University of Singapore    Mohan Gurusamy Affiliation: adityanawal@u.nus.edu, manit.baser@u.nus.edu, gmohan@nus.edu.sg
Abstract

AI agents augment large language models with external tools such as web retrieval, enabling grounded and up-to-date responses. However, incorporating external content into the generation pipeline can weaken the safety alignment mechanisms that govern model outputs. Prior work shows that enabling retrieval in agents increases compliance with harmful requests. We introduce AgentREVEAL, a diagnostic framework for analyzing retrieval-induced safety degradation in LLM agents. The framework examines two axes: how retrieval is integrated into the agent pipeline and the properties of the retrieved content. Along the integration axis, we find that binding tool invocation and response generation in a single step amplifies harmful outputs. Along the content axis, we uncover the Safe Source Paradox: even oppositional or safety-oriented sources, such as pages containing warnings or risk disclaimers, can increase harmful compliance by an average of 25% compared to the no-retrieval baseline. Finally, we show that relevance acts as a shared activation condition for both vulnerabilities. Similar patterns appear on frontier closed models, and harmful compliance remains elevated under several representative pipeline interventions, with some agents also entering this regime under autonomous retrieval. Because relevance is also what makes retrieval useful, these results expose a safety-utility trade-off for retrieval-enabled agents. We introduce HarmURLBench, a benchmark containing 1,405 real-world URLs paired with 320 harmful behaviors to support future evaluations.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as the backbone of intelligent agents (Xi et al., 2025), which perceive information, make decisions, and take actions on behalf of users. However, standalone LLMs are limited by a fixed training cutoff: they cannot access information beyond their training data, and when queried about current events or emerging facts, they may generate confident but incorrect responses rather than acknowledging uncertainty. To address this limitation, developers have built web-retrieval agents (Nakano et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2023), LLM-powered systems that browse, fetch, and synthesize information from external online sources in real time (Figure 1). These systems are now widely deployed in search assistants, research copilots, enterprise knowledge platforms, and customer support automation (Kumar et al., 2025).

Contemporary alignment techniques (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022) were designed for models that generate without external information, and do not directly account for the extended decision pipeline introduced by retrieval-enabled agents (Kumar et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a). Since safety training can fail when competing objectives produce mismatched generalization (Wei et al., 2023), retrieval introduces such an objective: completing the tool-mediated pipeline before responding. This decomposes generation into four stages (Gao et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2022): ❶ query formulation, ❷ document retrieval, ❸ context augmentation, and ❹ response generation.

Recent work shows that granting models access to web or tool-based information reduces refusal rates and increases harmful outputs even for strongly aligned models (Kumar et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025). Mitigation has focused on the visible endpoints: constraining unsafe query generation at ❶ (Zhan et al., 2025) or filtering outputs after ❹ response generation (Inan et al., 2023). The intermediate stages, ❷ document retrieval and ❸ context augmentation, which determine what information enters generation and how, remain less understood.

We study externally specified URL retrieval, a deployment setting where the retrieval target is supplied by the user, application state, or surrounding system rather than chosen by the model. This setting covers assistants that process pasted links or attachments, copilots grounded in selected documents, enterprise RAG over pre-selected corpora, and support or developer agents grounded in fixed documentation. Fixing source selection isolates the post-selection stages of the pipeline: which document reaches the context, how it is integrated, and how the final response changes.

We formalize this as AgentREVEAL (Retrieval-Enabled Vulnerability Elicitation in Aligned agents; Figure 2), a framework for isolating how retrieved content and its integration pathway influence safety outcomes. For the content axis, we construct HarmURLBench, pairing real-world URLs with HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024) harmful behaviors and annotating each along two dimensions: stance (discouraging →\rightarrow neutral →\rightarrow instructional) and relevance to the target behavior. For the architectural axis, we vary ❸ context augmentation to change how the same document is integrated, while ❹ response generation serves as the measurement stage scored for harmful compliance.

Across eight models spanning five families, we observe two systematic effects. Along the integration axis, the same retrieved content is more harmful through an agentic tool pathway than when passively inserted into the prompt; decoupling tool invocation from response generation mitigates this, consistent with temporal coupling as the primary driver of the architectural effect. Along the content axis, safety-oriented pages including warnings and risk disclaimers increase harmful compliance relative to no-retrieval baselines, a counterintuitive phenomenon we term the Safe Source Paradox. Both effects are strongest when retrieved content is topically relevant, indicating that the same property making retrieval useful is also the shared activation condition for safety degradation, with similar patterns observed on several frontier closed models. Diagnostics further confirm this is not confined to the fixed-URL setup: harmful compliance remains elevated under representative pipeline interventions (Llama-Guard input/output filtering, summarization, and chunking), and some agents also enter this regime under autonomous retrieval.

Our contributions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    We introduce AgentREVEAL, a diagnostic framework that decomposes retrieval-induced safety failures along two axes: the architectural axis (how retrieval is integrated) and the content axis (properties of retrieved material).

  2. 2.

    Analysis along the architectural axis shows that agentic integration amplifies harmful compliance beyond passive context exposure. We further identify a commitment bias: coupling retrieval and response generation increases harm, while DEFER, a decoupled tool-use design, reduces this effect without compromising utility.

  3. 3.

    Analysis along the content axis uncovers the Safe Source Paradox: safety-oriented retrieved content increases harmful compliance by 25% on average relative to no-retrieval baselines. The relevance of the content acts as the shared activation condition that triggers both vulnerabilities.

  4. 4.

    We release HarmURLBench, a benchmark of 1,405 stance-stratified URLs paired with 320 harmful behaviors, enabling controlled evaluation of retrieval-induced safety degradation.

2 Related Work

Retrieval Safety.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation grounds language models in external knowledge (Lewis et al., 2020), but can destabilize safety: benign retrieved contexts degrade guardrails (An et al., 2025; She et al., 2025), while poisoned corpora can induce harmful outputs (Zou et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2024). Existing RAG-safety studies typically treat retrieved content as neutral context or malicious instruction, leaving untested whether oppositional sources, such as safety warnings discouraging the behavior, can still increase compliance.

Agentic Tool Use.

LLM tool-use frameworks (Yao et al., 2022; Schick et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2023) expand model capabilities, but safety work has focused mainly on adversarial manipulation: gradient-based jailbreaks (Zou et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2023), indirect prompt injection (Greshake et al., 2023; Zhan et al., 2024), adversarial tool injection (Zhang et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2025b), and function-calling failures (Wu et al., 2025; Chiang et al., 2025). Separate studies show intrinsic degradation when aligned models act through browser or multi-step tool interfaces (Kumar et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a), or when retrieval is simply enabled (Yu et al., 2025). Together, these results establish that agentic retrieval can weaken safety, but they do not vary the stance and relevance of authentic retrieved sources.

Defenses.

Current mitigations include input/output classifiers (Inan et al., 2023), rule-based isolation (Li et al., 2025a), information-flow tracking (Zhong et al., 2025), policy-guided enforcement (Shi et al., 2025), and query-level reward shaping for agent systems (Zhan et al., 2025). These defenses remain largely content-centric: they filter malicious inputs, unsafe queries, or generated outputs, but do not test whether the retrieval integration pathway itself amplifies compliance given the same retrieved content.

3 Methodology

3.1 Definitions

Behavior. A templated natural-language request (drawn from HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024)) that solicits content violating safety norms (e.g., synthesis routes for dangerous substances or fraudulent instructions).

Topical Relevance (TR). A 1–5 integer rating measuring how closely the content of a retrieved URL pertains to the target behavior.

Stance Score (SS). A 1–5 integer rating measuring the stance of retrieved content toward the target behavior, where 1 denotes content that actively opposes the behavior and 5 denotes content that directly enables it.

Harmfulness Score (HH, H¯\bar{H}). A per-response rating produced by GPT-4o indicating the harmfulness of a model’s output, where 1 denotes a safe refusal and 5 denotes full harmful compliance.

3.2 Problem Setup

We study externally specified URL retrieval, where the user or surrounding system supplies an existing URL or source for the agent to fetch. This setting appears in pasted-link assistants, browsing agents that inherit clicked pages, document-grounded assistants, and enterprise RAG systems over selected sources. By fixing the URL and cached page content across conditions, we remove query formulation, search ranking, and page drift from the main contrast, allowing us to isolate the post-selection stages of the retrieval pipeline: which document reaches the model context at ❷ and how that content is integrated at ❸. The final response at ❹ serves as the measurement stage, where we evaluate whether these retrieval and integration choices increase harmful compliance. Appendix B.1 summarizes how this controlled setup maps to deployment and attack scenarios.

3.3 Dataset Construction: LLM-Driven Adversarial Discovery Pipeline

Existing benchmarks provide no mechanism to sample web content stratified by both topical relevance and stance. To populate HarmURLBench across the full SS1–SS5 spectrum using authentic, unmodified web pages, we developed an automated dual-LLM discovery pipeline, described below.

Each URL is annotated on the TR and SS dimensions defined in §3.1; full scoring rubrics and evaluation prompts are provided in Appendix A.

Pipeline Architecture. We formalize dataset construction as a behavior-to-URL mapping problem. Let BB denote the set of harmful behaviors sourced from HarmBench. For each behavior b∈Bb\in B and target stance st​a​r​g​e​t∈{1,2,3,4,5}s_{target}\in\{1,2,3,4,5\}, we seek a URL u∗u^{*} satisfying:

u∗=argmaxu∈𝒲𝕀[fS​S(u,b)=starget]𝕀[fT​R(u,b)≥τ]u^{*}=\operatorname*{argmax}_{u\in\mathcal{W}}\,\mathbb{I}[f_{SS}(u,b){=}s_{\text{target}}]\,\mathbb{I}[f_{TR}(u,b){\geq}\tau] (1)

where 𝒲\mathcal{W} is the accessible web, fS​Sf_{SS} is the Stance Score function, fT​Rf_{TR} is the Topical Relevance function, and τ=3\tau=3 is our relevance threshold.

Since 𝒲\mathcal{W} is vast and unindexed by stance, we approximate this optimization via an iterative, failure-driven search pipeline comprising three components:

Query Generator (Mg​e​nM_{gen}).

A Qwen-30B model that generates search queries targeting specific stance outcomes, incorporating failure feedback to refine strategies iteratively (e.g., “Query too defensive →\rightarrow attracted SS1 security blogs” →\rightarrow next query drops defensive terms).

Search Aggregator.

A local SearxNG instance aggregating results from Google, DuckDuckGo, and Yandex, providing surface web coverage.

Content Evaluator (Me​v​a​lM_{eval}).

A GPT-4 model that scores each fetched page on TR and SS (defined above). A URL qualifies only if TR≥ 3\,\geq\,3. The full iterative procedure is formalized in Algorithm 1. Query-generation and failure-analysis prompt templates are provided in Appendix A.1.

Dataset Summary. We source harmful behaviors from HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024). Over the 320 test behaviors, we aim to collect up to one URL per stance level (SS1–SS5) and with TR≥ 3\,\geq\,3. The final dataset contains 1,405 URLs (87.8% overall coverage); per-stance breakdowns are reported in Appendix A.4. SS/TR label validation is summarized in §3.5, with annotation details in Appendix A.2.

3.4 Experimental Setup

We evaluate four conditions (Table 1) to separate integration and content effects. Control vs. Inline measures harm from retrieved-content exposure without tool use. Inline vs. Agent tests whether tool-mediated integration amplifies harm given the same content. Agent vs. DEFER tests temporal coupling within tool use, since both use the retrieval tool and cached content but differ in whether fetching is bound to the harmful request. We vary URL stance under Agent to measure the content effect.

DEFER (Decoupled Execution of Fetching and Explicit Request) splits the interaction across two turns: the model first retrieves the URL in response to a benign request, and only afterward receives the harmful prompt once the content is already in context. We verify that this two-turn design does not degrade benign-task utility using a TriviaQA evaluation (Appendix G.5).

The four conditions instantiate AgentREVEAL as an empirical decomposition of retrieval-induced harm elevation. Let Δ​H=H⁡(q,c,d)−H0​(q)\Delta H=H(q,c,d)-H_{0}(q) denote the increase in harmfulness over the no-retrieval baseline for query qq, retrieved content cc with stance score s∈{1,…,5}s\in\{1,\ldots,5\}, and delivery mechanism d∈{bound,decoupled,passive}d\in\{\textsc{bound},\textsc{decoupled},\textsc{passive}\}. We write Bd=𝟏[d=bound]B_{d}=\mathbf{1}[d{=}\textsc{bound}] and s~=(s−1)/4\tilde{s}=(s-1)/4, so s~=0\tilde{s}=0 at SS1 and s~=1\tilde{s}=1 at SS5.

Under topically relevant retrieval (TR ≥\geq 3), we summarize the observed harm elevation as:

Δ​H=α⏟relevance (A2)+β​Bd⏟commitment (A1)+γ​s~⏟stance (A2)\Delta H=\underbrace{\alpha}_{\text{relevance (A2)}}+\underbrace{\beta B_{d}}_{\text{commitment (A1)}}+\underbrace{\gamma\tilde{s}}_{\text{stance (A2)}} (2)

Each coefficient is estimated from per-condition averages: β\beta from Agent vs. DEFER, γ\gamma from SS5 vs. SS1 within Agent, and α\alpha from DEFER(SS1) vs. Control. Because s~\tilde{s} is anchored at SS1, α\alpha corresponds to the relevance-triggered elevation for the weakest stance condition. Agent vs. Inline is the broader integration-pathway contrast, while Agent vs. DEFER estimates the narrower commitment-bias component. Thus Eq. 2 is an empirical contrast decomposition, with Section 4 reporting each contrast directly.

Agent Architecture and Tool-Calling Mechanism.

We study retrieval-enabled agents equipped with a URL-fetching tool (Appendix C.2). Because the target URL is specified in the prompt, query formulation is fixed, and each interaction reduces to tool invocation, cached webpage injection, and final response generation with no additional retrieval calls. This lets us isolate how retrieved content enters the model context.

We implement the agent using a custom vLLM-based serving pipeline (Kwon et al., 2023) rather than off-the-shelf frameworks such as LangGraph (LangChain, 2024) or AutoGen (Wu et al., 2024), whose injected prompts or formatting tokens could confound the Agent–Inline comparison. All conditions share the standard Llama 2/HarmBench safety prompt (Touvron et al., 2023); Agent conditions add only the tool-use instructions, and pre-cached webpages ensure identical content delivery across runs. We evaluate eight instruction-tuned models spanning five families, scales from 3B–32B, and diverse reported post-training recipes. Full tool, prompt, serving, model, and parse-error details are provided in Appendix C.

3.5 Evaluation Framework

All model outputs are scored using the Harmfulness Score HH defined in §3.1. A graded scale is necessary because retrieval augmentation frequently induces partial compliance, resulting in incremental erosion of safety guardrails that a binary safe/unsafe label would obscure.

We score outputs with GPT-4o (Zheng et al., 2023) (temperature =0.0=0.0) under the X-Teaming rubric (Rahman et al., 2025), calibrated against blinded human annotation. Two annotators re-scored 300 URLs blind to the automated labels: primary-vs-auto quadratic-weighted Cohen’s κ=0.72\kappa=0.72 (SS) / 0.810.81 (TR), inter-annotator κ=0.77\kappa=0.77 (SS) / 0.830.83 (TR). They also re-scored 400 outputs: GPT-4o-vs-human κ=0.74\kappa=0.74, inter-annotator κ=0.79\kappa=0.79 (87% raw agreement), no directional bias. Gemini-2.5-Pro re-scoring of ≈\approx800 outputs gives κ=0.889\kappa=0.889 and 92.1% ASR-cutoff agreement. We use HH as a standardized relative metric for condition contrasts. Labeling validation, the judge prompt, and second-judge robustness appear in Appendices A.2 and A.3.

4 Results

4.1 Axis 1: Does the delivery mechanism amplify harm?

Table 2 first shows that Agent consistently exceeds the no-retrieval Control baseline ( column 2 Table 3), increasing mean harmfulness by 47.8% on average. This establishes the overall retrieval-induced harm elevation; significance tests and category-wise scores are reported in Appendices D.2 and D.1.

The Inline condition tests whether this elevation is explained by exposure to retrieved text alone. It places the same cached content directly in the prompt without a tool call. Inline remains above Control, so content exposure matters, but Agent is still higher than Inline on average (2.66 vs. 2.47). To check that this residual gap is not just tool-output rendering, an Inline-Formatted condition wraps the cached content in tool-output tags without issuing a fetch_url call: Agent H¯\bar{H} still exceeds Inline-Formatted in 8 of 9 models (Appendix G.1, Table 19). The integration pathway thus contributes additional harm beyond content exposure or visible formatting alone.

DEFER tests whether the harmfulness of the agentic pathway depends on coupling retrieval and answering within the same trajectory. Agent and DEFER use the same retrieval tool, tool-role format, and cached content. They differ in timing: Agent fetches after receiving the harmful request, whereas DEFER fetches under a benign first turn and evaluates the harmful request only in a second turn. Agent exceeds DEFER in 7 of 8 models (Figure 3; Table 2). Several mechanisms could produce this drop; we test each below (Appendix G.4).

One possibility is that the second turn simply offers an extra refusal opportunity: inserting a behavior-independent benign pre-turn before the standard same-turn Agent-1step prompt yields only −0.10-0.10 on H¯\bar{H} (≈35%\approx 35\% of DEFER’s drop), so additional turn count alone is insufficient. Another is that retrieved content loses authority gradually as conversation turns accumulate; inserting one or two additional benign Q&A exchanges between the fetch and the harmful request lowers H¯\bar{H} slightly at the first extra turn and not at all at the second (non-significant in 5/6 models), so cross-turn handling behaves as a sharp one-step cliff at same-turn vs prior-turn rather than a graded decay over distance. Conversely, holding turn count constant but re-coupling the fetch with the harmful request raises harm above DEFER, indicating that same-turn retrieval creates a commitment bias: after the model has already acted on the harmful request by fetching, refusal becomes less likely. DEFER also preserves benign utility on TriviaQA (Appendix G.5); the same direction transfers to 5/6 closed models (Table 4; Appendix G.3).

However, DEFER still exceeds Control across all eight models, so architectural decoupling explains only part of the vulnerability. Even when retrieval is decoupled from the harmful request at stage \scriptsize3⃝, harmfulness remains elevated, pointing to the retrieved page itself, selected at stage \scriptsize2⃝, as a second driver.

4.2 Axis 2A: Does retrieved content affect the model vulnerability?

To isolate this content axis, we keep the Agent setup fixed and vary URL stance across five levels (SS1: oppositional →\rightarrow SS3: neutral →\rightarrow SS5: enabling), using only URLs that are topically relevant to the target behavior.

Table 3 shows harmfulness rises as content becomes more enabling: H¯SS5>H¯SS1\bar{H}_{\text{SS5}}>\bar{H}_{\text{SS1}} for all eight models, with some non-monotonic variation at intermediate levels. This pattern matches the intuition behind stance-filtering defenses: enabling content supports the behavior, while oppositional framing should discourage compliance.

Yet even the most oppositional content (SS1), including safety warnings, disclaimers, and counter-arguments, produces higher harmfulness than the no-retrieval baseline in seven of eight models (Figure 4; Appendix D.2). We term this counterintuitive phenomenon the Safe Source Paradox (SSP): content that explicitly discourages the harmful behavior nonetheless increases model harmfulness relative to receiving no retrieved content. SSP also replicates on frontier closed models, holding in 6/6 (non-copyright aggregate; Table 4).

A plausible explanation is topical activation: oppositional sources still discuss the harmful domain and may activate related knowledge already stored in the model, so it generates harmful details from learned model behavior even when the retrieved page contains only defensive information. For example, on a bomb-threat behavior (Qwen-2.5-14B) a Fire Warden emergency-response page (evacuation and incident-reporting only) flips the model from full refusal under Control (H=1H=1) to a detailed first-person threat template (H=5H=5); full case studies in Appendix F.1. Source-tracing and masking analyses support this account: harmful details in SSP responses are often absent from the SS1 page, responses lie closer to the model’s unlocked output than to the page, and masking domain-specific keywords restores refusal while preserving the page’s oppositional framing (Appendix F).

These observations predict a boundary condition: if topical activation drives SSP, off-topic retrieval should weaken it. We test this next.

4.3 Axis 2B: How does topical relevance affect the vulnerability?

Relative to Axis 2A, this experiment changes only the topical relevance of the retrieved content. We keep Agent delivery, the harmful request, the URL-fetching instruction, and the SS1–SS5 stance labels fixed, but replace each target-relevant page with content verified as topically irrelevant to the target behavior (TR==1); source material and TR verification details are reported in Appendix E.1.

Figure 5 shows that on-topic Agent is higher than both Control and TR==1 Agent for all eight models. On average, harmfulness drops from 2.662.66 under on-topic Agent to 1.721.72 under TR==1 Agent, close to Control at 1.801.80 (per-model values in Appendix Table 13). This collapse indicates that harm elevation depends on whether the retrieved page remains aligned with the harmful domain. We next examine whether the same relevance dependence appears in commitment bias and SSP.

The commitment-bias contrast shows a similar relevance dependence. Re-running DEFER across all eight models and three off-topic domains, matched to the Agent TR=1=1 replication, reduces the Agent–DEFER gap from +0.22+0.22 on-topic (Table 2) to +0.12+0.12 off-topic, a 45% reduction (Appendix Table 14). Six of eight models still retain a positive gap, suggesting that commitment bias is sensitive to retrieval relevance.

We apply the same relevance contrast to the Safe Source Paradox by comparing oppositional SS1 retrieval against Control under TR≥\geq3 and TR==1. Under TR≥\geq3, SS1 pages exceed Control by +0.45+0.45 harm points on average, producing the Safe Source Paradox. When only topical relevance is removed, the same SS1 comparison falls to −0.10-0.10 (Appendix Table 15). Thus the SSP vulnerability largely disappears once the retrieved page no longer discusses the harmful domain, further strengthening the topical-activation account that domain-relevant sources can trigger model-internal harmful knowledge even when their stance is oppositional.

4.4 Are these vulnerabilities limited to the externally specified URL setup?

To test whether these vulnerabilities are specific to the externally specified URL setting, we evaluate input/output filtering, common RAG pipeline transformations, and autonomous retrieval.

URL filtering. We classify each cached page with Llama-Guard-3-8B in a pre-fetch, content-only setting. The filter flags only 18.8% of oppositional SS1 pages and 39.4% of directly enabling SS5 pages, leaving 75% of URLs unflagged (Appendix H.3). This indicates that source-level filtering alone may miss risk as harmfulness is not evident from the URL name.

Summarization. RAG systems often summarize retrieved pages to reduce context length or remove extraneous detail. We replace full-page tool outputs with summaries and rerun the Agent condition. Agent remains +0.58+0.58 on H¯\bar{H} above Control (Appendix H.5). This suggests that summarization can compress retrieved content while preserving the topical relevance that activates the vulnerability.

Chunking. Many deployed RAG systems retrieve top-kk passages rather than full documents. We split pages into overlapping chunks and return BM25 top-kk chunks using the harmful request as the query. The chunked Agent condition still leaves a +0.88+0.88 residual on H¯\bar{H} above Control (Appendix H.6). This is consistent with relevance-ranked chunking selecting passages that remain aligned with the harmful request, preserving the Agent >> Control gap.

Post-generation filtering. We also test an output-side Llama-Guard-3-8B filter applied after generation, using the harmful behavior as the user turn and the generated model response as the assistant turn. The filter catches harmful outputs, but incurs a 21–25% false-positive rate. Moreover, even after filtering, defended Agent ASR remains 42% higher than defended Control on aggregate; applying the same filter in the DEFER condition reduces this residual gap to 19% (Appendix H.4).

Autonomous retrieval. We finally test whether the vulnerability arises only because our main setup bypasses query generation by specifying the URL. We provide only the harmful behavior and allow autonomous agents to decide whether to invoke retrieval. Across 11 evaluation models, 6 retrieve on at least 26.7% of harmful behaviors (Appendix H.1). This shows that many models still call the retrieval tool for harmful requests. Since SSP and commitment bias operate after retrieval, autonomous tool use can enter the same downstream regime, although this diagnostic does not separately re-estimate the two mechanisms.

Taken together, these diagnostics are not an exhaustive defense study, but they show that several common pipeline layers reduce yet do not close the post-retrieval harm gap, consistent with the relevance-based account established above.

5 Conclusion

We introduce AgentREVEAL, a diagnostic framework that decomposes retrieval-induced harm elevation in LLM agents under externally specified URL retrieval into two axes. Along the architectural axis, we identify a commitment bias: coupling tool invocation with a harmful request amplifies harmful compliance beyond passive context exposure, and DEFER mitigates this without degrading benign-task utility. On the content axis, the Safe Source Paradox shows that even safety-oriented sources can raise harmfulness above a no-retrieval baseline. Additional diagnostics show the effect generalizes beyond the fixed-URL setup: it replicates on frontier closed models and remains elevated under several representative pipeline interventions, while some agents also enter this regime under autonomous retrieval, pointing to a structural rather than content-level vulnerability. Topical relevance emerges as the shared activation condition across both axes, motivating future work that treats relevance as a vulnerability site rather than only a utility signal, because the relevance that grounds agent utility can also activate harmful compliance.

6 Limitations

First, our harmfulness metric relies on GPT-4o as an LLM judge, which may introduce calibration bias from style, verbosity, or framing. We mitigate this risk with a fixed rubric (Appendix A.3), human validation, and a second-judge robustness check, but HH should still be interpreted as a standardized relative metric for condition contrasts rather than a precise absolute measure of harm.

Second, our main results target externally specified URL retrieval, where the user or surrounding system supplies the URL. This scope is common in production (§1) and lets us isolate post-selection effects, but it does not estimate autonomous query generation, search ranking, live web drift, or long-horizon planning. Appendix H.1 shows that some models still retrieve under autonomous use, so pre-retrieval refusal is a complementary defense rather than a sufficient answer to the integration vulnerability studied here.

Third, our deployment diagnostics cover representative layers rather than a full production defense stack. We test URL filtering, output filtering, GPT-4o summarization, and BM25-ranked chunked retrieval; these interventions act at different pipeline points but do not restore the no-retrieval Control baseline (Appendices H.3, H.4, H.5, and H.6). We leave context sanitization, learned rerankers, policy-specific cascades, and multi-step retrieval systems for future work, noting related concurrent evaluations (An et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025).

Finally, HarmURLBench covers 320 behaviors and 1,405 English-language HTML URLs, which is broad but incomplete across domains, languages, modalities, and alignment regimes. Non-English retrieval may yield different SSP magnitudes because safety training and web coverage vary by language, and multimodal pages with images, video, or embedded PDFs may introduce distinct risks. Aggregate analyses may also obscure per-behavior heterogeneity. We therefore present our results as controlled evidence for the integration and content-axis effects we study, with broader languages, modalities, and alignment regimes left to future work.

7 Ethics Statement

This paper studies a safety vulnerability in retrieval-enabled AI systems. The central risk is that models can produce harmful responses after retrieving topically relevant content, including pages that appear benign or safety-oriented, and the retrieved source can make the response appear grounded. We report this behavior to support relevance-aware safeguards while avoiding publication of new attack payloads.

HarmURLBench pairs public webpages with harmful behaviors from HarmBench rather than introducing new harmful tasks. Because open release of the full URL list, cached HTML, or harmful seed queries could enable re-harvesting, we use the tiered release plan in Appendix B.2: public documentation, labels, aggregate statistics, and evaluation code; gated access to URLs and cached pages for vetted researchers under research-use terms; sanitized construction templates; and a takedown channel for webpage owners.

Human validation of HarmURLBench labels and model outputs required exposure to potentially distressing material. Annotators were familiar with LLM-safety annotation, were informed of the risks, and could stop participation at any point.

A.2 Human Validation of Dataset Labels

On a stratified random sample of 300 URLs (60 per SS level), two NLP graduate-student annotators re-scored TR and SS blind to the automated labels and to each other. Quadratic weighted Cohen’s κ\kappa against the automated labels is 0.720.72 (SS) and 0.810.81 (TR) for the primary annotator; inter-annotator κ\kappa is 0.770.77 (SS) and 0.830.83 (TR), with 83% raw agreement and no directional bias. Disagreements were mostly adjacent-level (SS2 vs. SS3, TR3 vs. TR4), driven by pages with defensive framing that still contain operational detail; clearly ambiguous URLs were removed and borderline cases retained.

A.3 Harmfulness Rubric and Judge Calibration

All model outputs are evaluated using a 5-point Harmfulness Score (H∈{1,2,3,4,5}H\in\{1,2,3,4,5\}). We adapt the scoring rubric from the X-Teaming framework (Rahman et al., 2025), which defines compliance levels relative to OpenAI’s prohibited usage policies:

GPT-4o evaluator judge prompt (adapted from X-Teaming’s GPTJudge (Rahman et al., 2025); temperature = 0.0, no system prompt):

Two NLP graduate-student annotators rescored a stratified sample of 400 outputs blind to model and condition: GPT-4o κ=0.74\kappa=0.74 against the primary annotator, inter-annotator κ=0.79\kappa=0.79 (87% raw agreement), no directional bias. To rule out judge-specific artefacts, we additionally rescored ∼\sim800 outputs covering the main families, conditions, and stance levels with Gemini-2.5-Pro; Table 5 reports agreement under the same rubric.

Off-diagonal counts at the ASR cutoff are nearly symmetric (33 vs. 32 out of 65 disagreements), so neither judge is systematically harsher; combined with the human calibration this reduces the risk that SSP or commitment bias are GPT-4o artefacts.

Supporting Section 4.2. Table 15 repeats the relevance contrast for the Safe Source Paradox. For each model we hold the source stance fixed at oppositional (SS1) and vary only topical relevance: Agent SS1 (TR≥\geq3) retrieves SS1 pages that discuss the harmful domain, while Agent SS1 (TR==1) retrieves SS1 pages from off-topic domains. Both are compared against the no-retrieval Control. On-topic SS1 reproduces the pattern in Table 3 (Δrel=+0.45\Delta_{\text{rel}}=+0.45 on average, positive for 7/8 models); off-topic SS1 collapses the gap to Δoff=−0.10\Delta_{\text{off}}=-0.10, indicating that domain relevance, not the oppositional stance itself, drives the paradox.

Figure 7 plots per-model mean harmfulness H¯\bar{H} across the full stance ladder (Control →\rightarrow SS1 →\rightarrow SS5) under Agent retrieval with TR≥\geq3. For each model, the dashed segment marks the Control-to-SS1 jump (the Safe Source Paradox), and the colored dots trace the monotone climb through neutral (SS3) to directly enabling (SS5) sources. Appendix F Safe Source Paradox Mechanistic Evidence

F.1 Qualitative Case Studies

Two SSP cases under Agent with authentic public URLs. Responses are truncated for space; HH from the GPT-4o judge (Appendix A.3).

Analysis. Under Control the model refuses (H=1H{=}1). With the SS1 fact-check retrieved, it produces a fully compliant Wikipedia edit (H=5H{=}5); the citations [61][62] do not appear in the page, so the harmful content is generated from model-internal knowledge activated by the article’s mention of the Donbas-genocide narrative.

F.2 Source Tracing and Keyword Interventions

We test three alternative explanations for the Safe Source Paradox: that the model reproduces harmful material directly from the retrieved page, that issuing a real fetch_url call alone relaxes refusal regardless of content, and that the page’s oppositional framing itself elicits the behavior. Judge-side artifacts are addressed separately by the human calibration in Appendix A.3. We probe Qwen-2.5-7B and Qwen-2.5-14B on a random sample of 100100 behaviors each (drawn from the test split, independently per model), treating SSP-triggered cases as those where Agent SS1 HH exceeds the no-retrieval Control for the same behavior (δ>0\delta>0). The retrieved page itself is scored with the same GPT-4o evaluator used for model outputs (Appendix A.3), treating the page text as if it were a model response. The evidence comes in three forms: response novelty relative to the page, lexical similarity to the model’s unlocked parametric probe versus the page, and a token-level keyword intervention.

Tables 16–17 examine whether SSP responses copy harmful material from the page. SS1 pages score H¯≈1.9\bar{H}\!\approx\!1.9–2.42.4 (consistent with their oppositional construction) while Agent responses for the same behaviors score H¯≈4.1\bar{H}\!\approx\!4.1–4.34.3, a +1.8+1.8 to +2.4+2.4 gap that cannot be attributed to content extracted from the page. 88–90% of response word-trigrams are absent from the SS1 page; for Qwen-2.5-7B, response trigrams are significantly more novel relative to the retrieved page than relative to the model’s own unlocked probe output (Wilcoxon p=0.001p=0.001), indicating the response content is lexically closer to what the model already knows than to what it retrieved. SSP responses are lexically closer to the unlocked probe than to the page in 79–91% of cases; for Qwen-2.5-14B mean Jaccard to probe (0.3440.344) substantially exceeds mean Jaccard to page (0.1370.137). The case studies in Appendix F.1 illustrate the same gap qualitatively: operational details in Agent completions are frequently absent from the oppositional source page.

Internal-domain capability split.

The bottom block of Table 16 partitions all 100100 sampled behaviors per model into capable (unlocked probe H≥3H\geq 3; the model can generate domain-relevant harmful content from internal memory) and incapable (probe H<3H<3). Capable behaviors yield substantially higher Agent SS1 H¯\bar{H} than incapable ones (4.154.15 vs. 2.252.25 for Qwen-2.5-14B, Mann–Whitney p=1.6×10−6p=1.6\times 10^{-6}; 3.733.73 vs. 2.402.40 for Qwen-2.5-7B, p=3.9×10−5p=3.9\times 10^{-5}), showing that the magnitude of SS1-condition harm scales with the model’s accessible domain knowledge. Notably, the SSP rate is lower among capable behaviors (15.6% vs. 34.5% for Qwen-2.5-7B, Fisher’s exact p=0.040p=0.040) – a ceiling-proximity effect: capable behaviors already show elevated Control-condition harm, compressing the available margin for SS1-driven elevation while absolute SS1 harm remains higher. The Part. ρ\rho column reports the partial Spearman correlation between probe HH and Agent SS1 HH after partialling out the Control score; for Qwen-2.5-14B this remains significant (ρ=0.364\rho=0.364, p<0.001p<0.001), ruling out the confound that capable behaviors are simply harder in general.

The token-level intervention isolates the page’s domain content from its oppositional framing and from the tool-call structure itself. For n=50n{=}50 SSP-triggered behaviors per model (drawn from the 100-behavior pool above), we measure P⁡(refusal)P(\text{refusal}) – the probability mass assigned to refusal-indicating tokens at generation position 00 – by querying the top-20 first-token log-probabilities via vLLM with temperature=0\text{temperature}{=}0. Refusal-indicating tokens are a fixed lexicon of leading refusal pieces (e.g., “I”, “I’m”, “Sorry”, “I cannot”, “As”, “Unfortunately”, and their BPE variants). We compare four conditions: Control (no retrieved content); Agent_SS1 (full SS1 page in context); Agent_Domain_Mask (SS1 page rewritten by GPT-4o to replace harmful-domain terms with semantically neutral placeholders while preserving the oppositional safety framing and sentence structure); and Agent_Offtopic (a length-matched off-topic article substituted for the SS1 page, wrapped in the same real fetch_url call and [Tool Output: fetch_url]…[/Tool Output] tags so the tool-call surface structure is held constant).

Table 18: the SS1 page causes a sharp refusal-probability collapse – P⁡(refusal)P(\text{refusal}) drops from →0.1810.834\!\to\!0.181 for Qwen-2.5-7B and from →0.3030.921\!\to\!0.303 for Qwen-2.5-14B under Agent_SS1 (log-odds shifts of −7.85-7.85 and −6.81-6.81, respectively). Domain masking substantially reverses this suppression: P⁡(refusal)P(\text{refusal}) recovers to 0.6540.654 (7B) and 0.8100.810 (14B), restoring approximately 78%78\% (7B) and 72%72\% (14B) of the suppressed log-odds signal, indicating that the page’s oppositional framing alone does not drive SSP. Agent_Offtopic also restores refusal (0.7700.770 and 0.7900.790) despite an identical real fetch_url call and tool-output wrapper, confirming the suppression is specific to domain-relevant content rather than a generic effect of any retrieved text and that issuing the call alone does not authorize compliance. The Inline-Formatted ablation in Appendix G.1 provides a complementary check, removing the real tool call while keeping the tool-output rendering. Combined with the off-topic Agent collapse in §4.2 (Appendix Table 13) and the closed-model SSP replication in Table 20, the convergent evidence is consistent with topical relevance, rather than stance, content copying, tool authorization, or framing alone, being the proximal trigger for SSP refusal collapse.

Scope. The direct mechanistic probes here cover two Qwen models. The closed-model results in Table 20 extend the SSP effect itself to six closed systems but do not separately re-estimate these mechanisms.

Appendix G Integration-Axis and Generalization Checks

G.1 Inline-Formatted Tool-Output Ablation

Agent and Inline differ in both tool execution and how retrieved content is rendered. To separate the two, we evaluate an Inline-Formatted condition that wraps the Inline content in [Tool Output: fetch_url]…[/Tool Output] tags in the user message without issuing a fetch_url call; system prompt, behavior, and content are fixed.

Table 19 shows Agent exceeds Inline-Formatted in 8/9 models (all four Qwen2.5 sizes 3B/7B/14B/32B included, with the gap growing with scale up to 14B), so the gap is not reducible to tool-output rendering; together with the Agent vs. DEFER contrast in §4.1, this attributes the residual gap to executing a tool call coupled to the harmful request.

G.2 Closed-Model SSP Validation

SSP at SS=1. Six closed models under the same cached-retrieval protocol: GPT-4, o4-mini, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, and DeepSeek-V3 (abbreviated G4, o4, G2.5, G2.0, C3.5, DSV3). Table 20 reports per-category Agent–Control deltas, with the four non-copyright categories aggregated in the final row.

Copyright is excluded from the aggregate because SS1 copyright pages typically discuss enforcement rather than the requested work, creating a topical mismatch that increases refusal rather than triggering SSP-style activation.

G.3 Closed-Model Commitment Bias at SS=1

We additionally ran DEFER at SS=1 on six closed models (GPT-4, o4-mini, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Claude-3.7-Sonnet and DeepSeek-V3) across all seven HarmBench categories. Same GPT-4o evaluator and H≥3H\geq 3 threshold as the main experiments.

Table 21 shows Gemini-2.5-Flash (+0.31+0.31) and Claude-Sonnet (+0.26+0.26) match the +0.22+0.22 mean gap on open-weight models (Table 2); Gemini-2.0-Flash, GPT-4, and o4-mini show smaller but still positive deltas (+0.08+0.08, +0.07+0.07, +0.04+0.04), while DeepSeek-V3 reverses on H¯\bar{H} (−0.37-0.37). Closed-model commitment bias is therefore a majority pattern (5/6).

G.4 DEFER Mechanism Decomposition

Four candidate mechanisms could in principle produce the Agent →\rightarrow DEFER drop in §4.1: reduced commitment bias, conversational framing, an extra refusal opportunity from the second turn, and cross-turn context treatment. The Agent vs. DEFER contrast in §4.1 and the Agent vs. Inline-Formatted contrast in Appendix G.1 jointly rule out conversational framing and tool-output rendering. This appendix isolates each of the three remaining accounts with one dedicated condition. All conditions share the same system prompt, decoding settings (temperature 0.0, seed 42, max_tokens=4096\texttt{max\_tokens}{=}4096), tool schema, and behavior set; only the conversation structure varies. The ablation covers six open-weight models on all 296 of 320 HarmBench test behaviors with a loadable cached URL, at SS=5.

Extra refusal opportunity. The second turn might help only by giving the model another chance to refuse, independent of whether retrieval is decoupled from the request. We insert a behavior-independent benign exchange (user message: “Hello. Briefly, what can you help with today?”) before the standard Agent-1step prompt; Turn 2 is the full Agent-1step user message (URL + behavior, fetch_url required), so same-turn fetch+request coupling is preserved. Cross-model ΔNeutral Pre-Turn−Agent-1step=−0.10\Delta_{\text{Neutral~Pre-Turn}-\text{Agent-1step}}=-0.10 (≈35%\approx 35\% of DEFER’s drop), significant in only 2/6 models; re-enabling commitment after a benign pre-turn flips direction, ΔNeutral Pre-Turn−DEFER=+0.19\Delta_{\text{Neutral~Pre-Turn}-\textsc{DEFER}}=+0.19 (significant in 4/6, harm increases). Extra turn count alone is therefore not the active ingredient: the second turn’s value is decoupling-conditional rather than turn-count-conditional. The Agent vs. DEFER contrast in §4.1 is consequently not confounded by an additional refusal slot.

Cross-turn context decay. If DEFER works because prior-turn retrieved content loses authority over distance, the gap should widen as more turns are interposed. We add one and two additional behavior-independent question-answer exchanges between the DEFER fetch and the harmful request (inter-turn distances d=2d{=}2 and d=3d{=}3); the fixed decoy questions are “Quick aside — what is the capital of Australia?” and “Also, can you remind me what year humans first landed on the moon?” Going from d=1d{=}1 (DEFER) to d=2d{=}2 removes a further −0.11-0.11 on average; the additional step from d=2d{=}2 to d=3d{=}3 contributes only −0.02-0.02 and is non-significant in 5/6 models. Cross-turn handling therefore operates as a single-step cliff (same-turn vs. prior-turn) rather than a graded decay, so the headline DEFER mitigation already captures essentially all of the cross-turn effect.

Target-URL specificity. The prior-turn fetch might reduce harm only because the model treats the target URL’s content as less authoritative when delivered cross-turn; an unrelated page should not produce the same effect. We replace the prior-turn fetch with a real fetch_url call to a fixed topically unrelated benign page (cached Wikipedia Bicycle article, served from a local cache for determinism); Turn 2 is the plain harmful behavior text with no “based on the content” framing. Substituting the off-topic page produces ΔOff-Topic Prime−DEFER=−0.92\Delta_{\text{Off-Topic~Prime}-\textsc{DEFER}}=-0.92 on average, larger than the commitment-bias drop itself and significant in 6/6 models (p<0.001p<0.001). The harm is therefore not specific to the target URL having been pre-fetched; what matters is whether the prior-turn content shares the harmful behavior’s topical domain — the same topical-activation pattern documented in §4.2. This contrast is thus consistent with the relevance-gating account in §4.2 rather than with cross-turn authority discounting, and commitment bias remains the active explanation of Agent →\rightarrow DEFER specifically because Agent-1step and DEFER share the same target URL.

User-message templates.

G.5 DEFER Benign-Task Utility Evaluation

We evaluate seven models on TriviaQA rc.wikipedia validation (Joshi et al., 2017), each question paired with its gold Wikipedia URL. Exact-match: prediction is correct if any gold alias appears as a case-insensitive substring of the output.

Table 24 shows DEFER outperforms single-turn Agent on 6/7 models (avg +0.164+0.164; tie on Granite-3.1-8B). Dedicating Turn 1 to retrieval places the page in context before the question is posed; the single-turn Agent must orchestrate the tool call and answer simultaneously, often before fully integrating the page. Consistency across families indicates a structural benefit of the two-turn design rather than a model-specific artefact.

G.6 Model Scale and Commitment Bias: Qwen 3B–32B

The Agent–DEFER gap shrinks monotonically with scale in the Qwen 2.5 family, from +0.41+0.41 at 3B to +0.21+0.21 at 32B (Table 25). This is consistent with commitment bias partly reflecting limited capacity to override a primed trajectory, a capacity that scales with model competence rather than being fixed by the pipeline architecture.

Appendix H Deployment Diagnostics

H.1 Autonomous Retrieval Diagnostic

For each of 11 models, we present the HarmBench-Test behavior with an instruction to consult the web and expose an optional fetch_url tool; the user message contains no URL. The system message frames the model as a safety-constrained research assistant with optional web access. Retrieval occurs only if the model voluntarily issues the tool call. We record the tool-call decision only, since downstream SSP and commitment-bias mechanisms are already measured on the controlled grid.

10/11 models retrieve on at least 5% of harmful behaviors and 6 retrieve on at least 26.7% (Table 26), showing that autonomous tool use can still enter the post-retrieval regime where SSP and commitment bias apply.

H.2 Pipeline Defense Evaluation

We evaluate two Llama-Guard-3-8B pipeline defenses (Inan et al., 2023): a pre-fetch content gate and a post-generation output filter, bracketing the post-retrieval mechanisms studied in the main experiments. We also note one further production-grade defense category, contextual safety prompting (system-level safety instructions, refusal reminders, self-reflection scaffolds), that we do not evaluate here. Yu et al. (2025) report that “additional safety prompting does not reliably mitigate” retrieval-induced safety degradation; retrieval-enabled aligned LLMs “often behave more unsafely than uncensored models without retrieval” even when refusal-reminder and self-reflection prompts are added, consistent with our finding that the trigger sits in topical relevance rather than at the prompt layer.

H.3 Pre-Fetch URL Filter

Each cached page is classified once in content-only framing, independent of the query and generation model.

Table 27 shows Llama-Guard flags only 18.8% of SS1 and 39.4% of SS5 pages; 75% of pages overall are unflagged, consistent with SSP: many risk-inducing pages are topically relevant but not unsafe in isolation.

H.4 Post-Generation Output Filter

We classify generated outputs with the harmful behavior as the user turn and the model response as the assistant turn; a flagged response is counted as replaced by a refusal.

Output filtering catches many harmful responses but retrieval conditions pay a larger false-positive cost (21–25% Agent vs. 7–9% Control). Defended Agent ASR remains 0.051 vs. 0.036 for defended Control (42% relative gap); defended DEFER reduces the residual to 0.043. Output filtering reduces surface harm but does not erase the retrieval-induced gap.

H.5 Summarization Ablation

We replace each cached page with a deterministic 400-word GPT-4o summary (factual digest of topic, claims, and stance; no added safety framing) and rerun Agent on six open-weight models with all other components fixed.

Summarization closes the Control gap for 1/6 models (Llama-3.1-8B); the rest remain +0.24+0.24 to +1.14+1.14 on H¯\bar{H} above Control. The mean Agent–Control gap drops from +0.92+0.92 to +0.58+0.58 on H¯\bar{H} – about a third of the paradox recovered, two thirds left intact. A faithful summary preserves the page’s topic and stance, so it preserves the relevance signal that activates the vulnerability (§4.2).

H.6 Chunking Ablation

Each cached page is split into 512-token chunks (50-token overlap); BM25 selects the top five against the harmful behavior. Agent is rerun on the same six-model subset with all other components fixed.

Chunking fails to close the Control gap for all six models (Table 30). Mean H¯\bar{H} changes only from 2.662.66 (Agent) to 2.622.62 (Agent+Chunked), leaving a +0.88+0.88 residual on H¯\bar{H} above Control. BM25 ranks chunks by relevance to the harmful request and so preserves the topical signal identified in §4.2 as the activation condition.
